title: Neuropsychiatric manifestations of anti‐N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate receptor encephalitis in a 14‐year‐old female: A case report
case_prompt: A previously healthy 14-year-old girl presented with sudden-onset fever and an altered level of consciousness. Over the next 4 days, she was treated empirically for presumed viral encephalitis. On hospital day 6, she developed right-sided weakness, an inability to speak, repetitive behaviors, and visual hallucinations. She had no significant past medical or travel history. Routine blood counts and a noncontrast head CT scan were unremarkable, and electroencephalography showed no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a mild elevation of protein with lymphocytic predominance. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral temporal lobe enhancement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral encephalitis was considered given the fever and altered consciousness but was made less likely by normal imaging and neurophysiologic studies — “CBC and CT scans of the brain were unremarkable. EEG showed no changes.”  
2. Postinfectious encephalitis was included in the initial differential because of the preceding febrile illness and subsequent neurological decline — “Differential diagnoses included viral, autoimmune and postinfectious encephalitis and psychiatric illness.”  
3. Primary psychiatric illness was considered due to visual hallucinations and repetitive behaviors but was not supported by objective neurologic deficits and CSF findings — “Differential diagnoses included viral, autoimmune and postinfectious encephalitis and psychiatric illness.”  
4. Contactin-associated protein-like 2–mediated encephalitis was excluded by a negative CSF antibody assay — “Anti‐contactin‐associated protein‐like 2 Negative”  
5. AMPA receptor (type AMPA1/2) encephalitis was ruled out by negative autoantibodies in CSF — “Glutamate Receptor (type AMPA1/2) Negative”  
6. LGI1 antibody–mediated encephalitis was excluded on the basis of a negative CSF test — “Leucine‐rich glioma inactivated protein 1 (LGI1) Negative”  
7. GABA-b receptor encephalitis was excluded because CSF testing did not detect GABA-b antibodies — “GABA‐b receptor Negative”  
8. Dipeptidyl-aminopeptidase-like protein 6 encephalitis was ruled out by a negative CSF assay — “Dipeptidyl‐aminopeptidase‐like protein 6 Negative”
